text:
For this benchmark, a suitable uncertainty diagnostic is a stratified paired user bootstrap: record each user’s binary hit for both models, resample 200 users with replacement within each dataset using identical indices for both models, then average the four dataset-level HR differences. Report the observed macro difference, a 95% bootstrap interval, and per-dataset differences. One additional hit changes dataset HR by 0.5 percentage points and macro HR by 0.125 points. This procedure applies user-level statistical comparison principles discussed in [Cañamares et al.](https://doi.org/10.1007/s10791-020-09371-3); it assumes users are independent sampling units and conditions on the four datasets and fitted models.

Repeated configuration and checkpoint comparisons can overfit validation noise: the winning score is optimistically selected. A bootstrap interval computed after choosing that winner does not correct adaptive selection bias. [Cawley and Talbot](https://jmlr.csail.mit.edu/beta/papers/v11/cawley10a.html) show that selection effects can rival differences between algorithms. Practical implications: predeclare checkpoint/comparison rules, record every comparison, treat small selected gains as exploratory, and reserve independent evaluation for the frozen choice. A validation interval excluding zero alone does not establish improvement after adaptive search.

Fixed negative candidates support consistent paired comparisons but leave candidate-sampling uncertainty unmeasured. HR@10 among 100 candidates measures that sampled ranking task; it cannot establish full-catalog HR@10 improvement. [Krichene and Rendle](https://www.ijcai.org/proceedings/2021/0651.pdf) show sampled metrics can reverse model rankings, even in expectation. Likewise, user bootstrapping with training seed 42 does not measure initialization or training-sampling variability. Under the pinned protocol, describe gains as conditional on the split, candidate realization, and training seed; cross-seed robustness remains untested.
